title: Reactive Intravascular Plasmablastic/Immunoblastic Proliferation in a Patient with Concurrent Gastric Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue Lymphoma and Tuberculosis Potentially Mimicking Aggressive Intravascular Lymphoma: A Rare Case Report
case_text: A 79-year-old female presenting with upper abdominal discomfort, weight loss and weakness for 3 months was admitted in our hospital. The patient, a long-term rural farmer, reported a medical history of hypertension, kidney stones and gastritis with prior use of antihypertensive medications and proton pump inhibitors. She denied diabetes, coronary heart disease, HIV/HBV infection, family malignancies, surgeries, smoking, or alcohol abuse. No fever, night sweats, and superficial lymphadenopathy were noted. Subsequent hematological tests revealed the hypoproteinemia, and enhanced CT scan and ultrasound indicated gastric malignancy, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathies and polyserosal effusions, including pericardial effusion, pleural effusion, pelvic effusion, and ascites. H.P. was not detected by C14 urea breath test. Then the patient underwent a gastric endoscopy examination. Mucosal erosion and thickening, and superficial cobblestone lesions in the anterior wall of gastric body were observed macroscopically (Fig. 1). The endoscopic biopsy specimen was sent to pathology laboratory. Histologically, a large number of uniformly small to medium-sized lymphocytes infiltrated the lamina propria (shown in Fig. 2a) with prominent lymphoepithelial lesions (shown in Fig. 2b, c), reduced mucosal glands and focally epithelioid granuloma. Notably, extensive intralymphovascular lesions were also observed. Abundant large-sized plasmablasts or immunoblasts aggregated and completely filled the lumen of vessels and expanded the vessels in the lamina propria (shown in Fig. 3a, b). The summary of IHC interpretation in the intralymphovascular and extralymphovascular lymphoid cells is listed in Table 1. Briefly, the intralymphovascular large lymphoid cells were positive for CD79alpha, MUM1/IRF4, whereas negative for CD20, CD138, PAX5, CD30, Bcl-2, Bcl-6, C-myc by immunostaining (shown in Fig. 3a, b). CD34 highlighted the blood vessels (shown in Fig. 3a). Immunoglobulin light chain restriction was not detected by Kappa and Lambda immunostaining, and Ki67 positivity was more than 80% in the intravascular large lymphoid cells (shown in Fig. 3b). EBER was not detected by ISH. Furthermore, monoclonal rearrangements in IgH, IgK, and IgL genes were detected by PCR. In combination with IHC and genetic results, the diagnosis of MALT lymphoma with possible RIVPIP was supported. However, MALT lymphoma, as an indolent lymphoma, seemed to be incompatible with the patient's systemic symptoms. Aggressive intravascular lymphoma cannot still be completely excluded. Retrospectively, the patient had a history of endoscopic biopsy in the same site and omeprazole intake 2 months ago. Therefore, previous H&E sections from another hospital were requested to consult and review. Unexpectedly, conspicuous caseous necrosis, epithelioid granulomas (shown in Fig. 4a), multinucleated giant cells (shown in Fig. 4b), and two acid-fast Bacilli were found in her previous biopsy, highly suggestive of tuberculosis, but the initial diagnosis referred to chronic granulomatous inflammation. Additionally, the infiltration of a great number of small lymphoid cells in the lamina propria but no intravascular lesions were observed. Based on two biopsy specimens and clinical manifestations, the case was eventually diagnosed as concurrent gastric MALT lymphoma and tuberculosis with RIVPIP. After 4 weeks of targeted antibiotic therapy for both H.P. and M.T., the patient's abdominal discomfort subsided and tuberculous infection-associated polyserosal effusions significantly diminished, accompanied by improved appetite.
